title: Ἡ Πηνελόπεια ἀπιστεῖ
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Book 23 opens with the nurse Eurycleia climbing to the upper rooms, laughing aloud, to tell Penelope that Odysseus is home and the suitors are dead. Penelope, woken from a deep sleep, will not credit it: she tells the old woman that the gods have made her mad, and that any other servant who woke her with such talk would have been sent away sharply. Eurycleia insists, and Penelope, half-persuaded, springs up weeping and asks for the whole story. The nurse says only what she heard from the closed women's rooms and what she saw when Telemachus called her: Odysseus standing among the heaped dead, fumigating the house. Penelope still holds back and suspects that one of the gods killed the suitors, and that Odysseus is lost. Eurycleia reminds her of the scar from the boar's tusk and stakes her own life on the news. Penelope agrees to go down, torn between questioning her husband from a distance and embracing him. She enters, sits opposite him in the firelight, and says nothing, while he sits by a pillar waiting, and Telemachus begins to rebuke her.

sentences.t:
γρηῢς δ’ εἰς ὑπερῷ’ ἀνεβήσετο καγχαλόωσα,
δεσποίνῃ ἐρέουσα φίλον πόσιν ἔνδον ἐόντα·
sentences.tr:
grēÿs d’ eis hyperōi’ anebēseto kanchaloōsa,
despoinēi ereousa philon posin endon eonta·
sentences.l:
The old woman up to the upper rooms went up, exulting,
to her mistress to say that her dear husband was within;
sentences.i: The old woman went up to the upper rooms, exulting, to tell her mistress that her dear husband was in the house;
sentences.n: γρηῢς is the Ionic form of Attic γραῦς, 'old woman'; she is Eurycleia, not named until line 25. καγχαλόωσα is a participle of καγχαλάω 'laugh aloud, exult', with the open ending -όωσα (Attic -ῶσα). ὑπερῷ’ is elided ὑπερῷα, 'the upper rooms', where Penelope has been asleep; εἰς with the accusative gives 'up into'. ἀνεβήσετο is an aorist of ἀναβαίνω 'go up' with a middle ending and active sense. ἐρέουσα is a future participle of ἐρέω 'say', expressing purpose, and δεσποίνῃ is the person it is said to. In φίλον πόσιν ἔνδον ἐόντα, ἐόντα is Ionic for ὄντα, and φίλον is the stock 'dear', kept in the translation every time.

sentences.t: γούνατα δ’ ἐρρώσαντο, πόδες δ’ ὑπερικταίνοντο.
sentences.tr: gounata d’ errōsanto, podes d’ hyperiktainonto.
sentences.l: And her knees moved-briskly, her feet were quickened-above.
sentences.i: Her knees moved briskly and her feet hurried on.
sentences.n: ἐρρώσαντο is an aorist middle of ῥώομαι 'move swiftly, dart'. ὑπερικταίνοντο is an imperfect middle and the word occurs only here; its exact sense is not known. 'Were quickened' is a guess from the context, and the l shows the prefix ὑπερ- as '-above' without claiming that it means that here. γούνατα and πόδες are the subjects of two short clauses set side by side with δέ … δέ, each with its own verb: the line is a quick pair, matching the old woman's haste.

sentences.t: στῆ δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπὲρ κεφαλῆς καί μιν πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπεν·
sentences.tr: stē d’ ar’ hyper kephalēs kai min pros mython eeipen·
sentences.l: and she stood then above her head, and to her spoke a word:
sentences.i: She stood over her head and spoke to her:
sentences.n: The line repeats 4.803 (the second line of the unit that begins at 4.802), and the English follows that line except for the speaker. στῆ is the unaugmented aorist of ἵστημι (Attic ἔστη). In πρὸς … ἔειπεν the preverb stands apart from the verb (tmesis), and μῦθον is an inner object: 'spoke a word to her'. μιν is 'her', a pronoun for a person not named in the line. The text prints no comma after κεφαλῆς here.

sentences.t:
ἔγρεο, Πηνελόπεια, φίλον τέκος, ὄφρα ἴδηαι
ὀφθαλμοῖσι τεοῖσι τά τ’ ἔλδεαι ἤματα πάντα.
sentences.tr:
egreo, Pēnelopeia, philon tekos, ophra idēai
ophthalmoisi teoisi ta t’ eldeai ēmata panta.
sentences.l:
“Wake, Penelope, dear child, so that you may see
with your eyes what you long for all your days.
sentences.i: “Wake, Penelope, dear child, and see with your own eyes what you have longed for all your days.
sentences.n: ἔγρεο is the aorist imperative middle of ἐγείρω, 'wake up!' (the root of ἀνεγείρεις in line 16). ἴδηαι is the aorist subjunctive, 2 sg., in the older ending -ηαι (Attic ἴδῃς), after ὄφρα 'so that' of purpose. Πηνελόπεια is the vocative. φίλον τέκος, 'dear child', is how the old nurse addresses her mistress; τέκος is neuter and φίλον agrees with it. τεοῖσι is the dative plural of τεός, Ionic for σός 'your', and ὀφθαλμοῖσι ends in -οισι. τά τ’ ἔλδεαι: τά is the relative 'what', τε the epic particle, and ἔλδεαι the 2 sg. of ἔλδομαι 'long for'. ἤματα πάντα 'all days' is a fixed phrase.

sentences.t: ἦλθ’ Ὀδυσεὺς καὶ οἶκον ἱκάνεται, ὀψέ περ ἐλθών.
sentences.tr: ēlth’ Odyseus kai oikon hikanetai, opse per elthōn.
sentences.l: Odysseus has come and is reaching his house, late though he came.
sentences.i: Odysseus has come: he is reaching his house, late as his coming is.
sentences.n: ἦλθ’ is elided ἦλθε. Ὀδυσεύς has one σ here; the form with two (Ὀδυσσεύς) stands in line 18, and the poet takes whichever fits the verse. ἱκάνεται, 'reaches', is a present with a middle ending (Attic ἱκνεῖται): the arrival is still happening as she speaks. ὀψέ is the adverb 'late', and περ with the participle ἐλθών gives it concessive force: 'late though he came'.

sentences.t:
μνηστῆρας δ’ ἔκτεινεν ἀγήνορας, οἵ θ’ ἑὸν οἶκον
κήδεσκον καὶ κτήματ’ ἔδον βιόωντό τε παῖδα.
sentences.tr:
mnēstēras d’ ekteinen agēnoras, hoi th’ heon oikon
kēdeskon kai ktēmat’ edon bioōnto te paida.
sentences.l:
And the lordly suitors he killed, who his own house
used-to-harm and goods ate and did-violence-to his son.”
sentences.i: He has killed the lordly suitors, who kept harming his house, ate his goods and did violence to his son.”
sentences.n: ἀγήνορας, 'lordly', is the stock epithet of the suitors and is translated every time; here it stands after its noun and so is emphatic. ἑόν is the possessive 'his own', not the relative. The three verbs, κήδεσκον, ἔδον and βιόωντο, are all imperfects and name the suitors' standing crimes; κήδεσκον is an iterative form (-σκον) of κήδω 'trouble, harm', ἔδον is the unaugmented imperfect of ἐσθίω 'eat', and βιόωντο is a middle with open endings (Attic ἐβιῶντο) of βιάομαι 'do violence to'. κτήματα are 'possessions, goods'.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε περίφρων Πηνελόπεια·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ aute proseeipe periphrōn Pēnelopeia·
sentences.l: Her then in turn addressed circumspect Penelope:
sentences.i: Then circumspect Penelope spoke to her in turn:
sentences.n: This is the formula that introduces Penelope's reply, and it repeats 4.830; the English is the same each time. τήν, 'her', is the article used as a pronoun; αὖτε means 'in turn, again'. The epithet περίφρων, 'circumspect', is translated every time, and its second half is φρήν, 'mind': she is the woman who looks around.

sentences.t:
μαῖα φίλη, μάργην σε θεοὶ θέσαν, οἵ τε δύνανται
ἄφρονα ποιῆσαι καὶ ἐπίφρονά περ μάλ’ ἐόντα,
καί τε χαλιφρονέοντα σαοφροσύνης ἐπέβησαν·
sentences.tr:
maia philē, margēn se theoi thesan, hoi te dynantai
aphrona poiēsai kai epiphrona per mal’ eonta,
kai te chaliphroneonta saophrosynēs epebēsan·
sentences.i: “Dear nurse, the gods have made you mad, they who can make a fool even of one who is very thoughtful, and who can set even the light-minded on good sense;
sentences.n: μαῖα is a courteous address to an older woman, and here the woman is the nurse; the English is 'dear nurse' every time μαῖα φίλη is said to her. The separate word τροφός, in φίλη τροφός, is also 'nurse'. μάργην is 'mad, frantic'. The first clause rests on the verb θέσαν, the unaugmented aorist of τίθημι 'make'. ἄφρονα and ἐπίφρονα are opposites built on φρήν: 'senseless' and 'thoughtful'. καί τε χαλιφρονέοντα has the epic particle τε marking a general truth; the gods can do the opposite also. ἐπέβησαν is a transitive aorist, 'set upon', with σαοφροσύνης in the genitive. σαοφροσύνη is 'sound-mindedness', from σάος 'safe' and φρήν.

sentences.t: οἵ σέ περ ἔβλαψαν·
sentences.tr: hoi se per eblapsan·
sentences.l: they have harmed even you;
sentences.i: they have harmed even you;
sentences.n: οἵ is a relative used as a connective: 'and they', picking up θεοί. σέ περ 'you also, even you' is the point: the gods' power reaches the wisest. ἔβλαψαν is the aorist of βλάπτω 'harm, hinder'.

sentences.t: πρὶν δὲ φρένας αἰσίμη ἦσθα.
sentences.tr: prin de phrenas aisimē ēstha.
sentences.l: but before, as to your wits, you were fitting.
sentences.i: but until now you were sound in your wits.
sentences.n: πρίν is 'before, formerly'; δέ here is 'but'. ἦσθα is 'you were', the old 2 sg. imperfect of εἰμί. φρένας is an accusative of respect, 'as to your wits'. αἴσιμος is built on αἶσα 'portion, due share', so it means 'in due measure, fitting', and so 'sound'.

sentences.l:
Why do you mock me, having a heart of much grief,
these things beyond-the-mark saying, and from sleep do you rouse me
sweet, which bound me, covering about my dear eyelids?
sentences.i: Why do you mock me, with a heart so full of grief, saying such things beyond the mark, and rouse me from the sweet sleep that bound me and shrouded my dear eyelids?
sentences.n: τίπτε is τί ποτε 'why ever'. λωβεύεις is 'treat with contempt, mock'. πολυπενθέα is accusative singular masculine of πολυπενθής 'very sorrowful', agreeing with θυμόν; ἔχουσαν agrees with με. παρέξ is 'outside, beyond'; ταῦτα παρὲξ ἐρέουσα is read as 'saying these things beyond the mark', outside what is true or fitting. That is the best reading of the phrase, not a certain one. ἀνεγείρεις carries on the 'wake' of ἔγρεο in line 5. The relative clause ὅς μ’ ἐπέδησε says that sleep 'bound' her: ἐπέδησε is an aorist of ἐπιδέω, and ἀμφικαλύψας is the aorist participle of ἀμφικαλύπτω 'cover all round'. φίλα βλέφαρα, 'dear eyelids', keeps the stock φίλος where it means 'one's own'.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ πω τοιόνδε κατέδραθον, ἐξ οὗ Ὀδυσσεὺς
ᾤχετ’ ἐποψόμενος Κακοΐλιον οὐκ ὀνομαστήν.
sentences.tr:
ou gar pō toionde katedrathon, ex hou Odysseus
ōichet’ epopsomenos Kakoïlion ouk onomastēn.
sentences.l:
For not yet have I slept such a sleep, since Odysseus
went off to look on Evil-Ilium, not to be named.
sentences.i: For I have never yet slept like this since Odysseus went off to look on Evil-Ilium, a place not to be named.
sentences.n: γάρ gives the reason for her anger: she has not slept so soundly since he left. κατέδραθον is the aorist of καταδαρθάνω 'fall asleep'; τοιόνδε is an accusative used as an inner object, 'such a sleep'. ἐξ οὗ means 'from the time when'. ᾤχετ’ is the imperfect of οἴχομαι 'be gone, go off', and ἐποψόμενος a future participle of purpose, 'to look upon'. Κακοΐλιον, 'Evil-Ilium', is Penelope's name for Troy, built on κακός and Ἴλιος; and οὐκ ὀνομαστήν means 'not to be named'. This line repeats 19.260, also spoken by Penelope.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγε νῦν κατάβηθι καὶ ἂψ ἔρχευ μέγαρόνδε.
sentences.tr: all’ age nyn katabēthi kai aps ercheu megaronde.
sentences.l: But come now, go down and go back again to the hall.
sentences.i: But come now, go down, and go back to the hall.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε νῦν is 'but come now', a spur to action. κατάβηθι is the aorist imperative of καταβαίνω. ἔρχευ is the imperative middle of ἔρχομαι (Attic ἔρχου). ἂψ is 'back again'. μέγαρόνδε is μέγαρον with the suffix -δε, 'to the hall'; the suffix marks direction.

sentences.t:
εἰ γάρ τίς μ’ ἄλλη γε γυναικῶν, αἵ μοι ἔασι,
ταῦτ’ ἐλθοῦσ’ ἤγγειλε καὶ ἐξ ὕπνου ἀνέγειρεν,
τῷ κε τάχα στυγερῶς μιν ἐγὼν ἀπέπεμψα νέεσθαι
αὖτις ἔσω μέγαρον·
sentences.tr:
ei gar tis m’ allē ge gynaikōn, hai moi easi,
taut’ elthous’ ēngeile kai ex hypnou anegeiren,
tōi ke tacha stygerōs min egōn apepempsa neesthai
autis esō megaron·
sentences.l:
For if some other of the women, those who are mine,
had come and reported these things and wakened me from sleep,
her soon harshly I would have sent away to go
back again into the hall;
sentences.i: For if any other of the women of my household had come and brought me this news and woken me from sleep, I would soon have sent her off harshly to go back into the hall;
sentences.n: The sentence is a contrary-to-fact condition in the past, with the aorist indicative in both halves: εἰ … ἤγγειλε … ἀνέγειρεν, 'if she had reported and woken', and then τῷ κε … ἀπέπεμψα, 'then I would have sent away'. αἵ μοι ἔασι, 'who are mine', uses ἔασι, the epic form of εἰσί. ἤγγειλε is an aorist of ἀγγέλλω 'report'. τῷ here means 'in that case'. τάχα is 'quickly, soon'. στυγερῶς is 'in a hateful way, harshly'. νέεσθαι is the uncontracted infinitive of νέομαι 'go' (Attic νεῖσθαι), and ἔσω with the accusative means 'into'.

sentences.t: σὲ δὲ τοῦτό γε γῆρας ὀνήσει.
sentences.tr: se de touto ge gēras onēsei.
sentences.l: but you this old age at least will benefit.”
sentences.i: but this old age of yours, at least, will profit you.”
sentences.n: σὲ δὲ τοῦτό γε γῆρας ὀνήσει is the end of her sharp speech, and it turns: her age will spare the nurse what a younger woman would suffer. ὀνήσει is the future of ὀνίνημι 'benefit, profit'; τοῦτο … γῆρας means 'this old age of yours', with the demonstrative standing for the possessive.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε φίλη τροφὸς Εὐρύκλεια·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ aute proseeipe philē trophos Eurykleia·
sentences.l: Her then in turn addressed the dear nurse Eurycleia:
sentences.i: Then her dear nurse Eurycleia spoke to her in turn:
sentences.n: This line repeats 4.742. φίλη τροφός, 'dear nurse', is the nurse's fixed epithet and is translated every time. τροφός is 'nurse', the one who brings up a child. Eurycleia gets her name here for the first time in this part.

sentences.t:
οὔ τί σε λωβεύω, τέκνον φίλον, ἀλλ’ ἔτυμόν τοι
ἦλθ’ Ὀδυσεὺς καὶ οἶκον ἱκάνεται, ὡς ἀγορεύω,
ὁ ξεῖνος, τὸν πάντες ἀτίμων ἐν μεγάροισι.
sentences.tr:
ou ti se lōbeuō, teknon philon, all’ etymon toi
ēlth’ Odyseus kai oikon hikanetai, hōs agoreuō,
ho xeinos, ton pantes atimōn en megaroisi.
sentences.l:
“In no way do I mock you, dear child, but in truth
Odysseus has come and is reaching his house, as I declare,
the stranger, whom all were dishonouring in the halls.
sentences.i: “I am not mocking you, dear child. It is true, as I tell you: Odysseus has come and is reaching his house, the stranger whom all were dishonouring in the halls.
sentences.n: τέκνον φίλον is 'dear child', the same address as φίλον τέκος in line 5, with the words in the other order. οὔ τί σε λωβεύω answers her mistress's λωβεύεις in line 15. ἔτυμόν is 'true' (used as an adverb here) and τοι is the dative of σύ, 'to you'. The first half of the second line, ἦλθ’ Ὀδυσεὺς καὶ οἶκον ἱκάνεται, repeats the first half of line 7 word for word. ὡς ἀγορεύω is 'as I say'. ὁ ξεῖνος, 'the stranger', is the beggar whom all in the halls had been dishonouring; Eurycleia names him by the guise in which he was known there. ἀτίμων is the imperfect 3 pl. of ἀτιμάω 'dishonour', without augment.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχος δ’ ἄρα μιν πάλαι ᾔδεεν ἔνδον ἐόντα,
ἀλλὰ σαοφροσύνῃσι νοήματα πατρὸς ἔκευθεν,
ὄφρ’ ἀνδρῶν τίσαιτο βίην ὑπερηνορεόντων.
sentences.tr:
Tēlemachos d’ ara min palai ēideen endon eonta,
alla saophrosynēisi noēmata patros ekeuthen,
ophr’ andrōn tisaito biēn hyperēnoreontōn.
sentences.l:
And Telemachus, you see, had known him long since to be within,
but by sound-mindednesses hid his father's thoughts,
so that he might exact payment for the force of the over-bold men.”
sentences.i: Telemachus had known long since that he was in the house, but in his prudence he kept his father's plans hidden, so that he might punish the violence of the overbearing men.”
sentences.n: ἄρα here is a particle of surprise or plain statement, 'you see'. ᾔδεεν is the pluperfect of οἶδα, 'had known' (Attic ᾔδει). πάλαι is 'long ago'. σαοφροσύνῃσι is a plural dative, 'by his prudences', that is by taking care; it picks up σαοφροσύνης from line 13. νοήματα are 'thoughts, intentions'. ἔκευθεν is the imperfect of κεύθω 'hide'. ὄφρα with the optative τίσαιτο gives the purpose, which lay in the past: τίσαιτο is the aorist optative middle of τίνω 'exact payment', its object βίην 'force, violence'. ὑπερηνορεόντων 'over-bold men' is the participle used of the Cyclopes in book 6, and is a reproach.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, ἡ δ’ ἐχάρη καὶ ἀπὸ λέκτροιο θοροῦσα
γρηῒ περιπλέχθη, βλεφάρων δ’ ἀπὸ δάκρυον ἧκεν·
καί μιν φωνήσασ’ ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr:
hōs ephath’, hē d’ echarē kai apo lektroio thorousa
grēï periplechthē, blepharōn d’ apo dakryon hēken·
kai min phōnēsas’ epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.i: So the nurse spoke, and Penelope was glad, and sprang from her bed and clung about the old woman, and let a tear fall from her eyelids; and, raising her voice, she spoke winged words to her:
sentences.n: ἔφαθ’ is ἔφατο with its τ turned to θ before the rough breathing of ἡ; it is the imperfect middle of φημί, 'she said'. ἡ δ’ is 'and she', Penelope, the article used as a pronoun. ἐχάρη is the aorist passive of χαίρω 'rejoice'. θοροῦσα is the aorist participle of θρῴσκω 'leap'. γρηῒ is the dative of γρηῦς (see line 1). περιπλέχθη, 'was entwined about', is a passive form of περιπλέκω, with the dative of what she clung to. In βλεφάρων δ’ ἀπὸ the preposition stands after its noun. ἧκεν is the aorist of ἵημι 'send, let fall'. The last line of this unit, καί μιν φωνήσασ’ ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα, is the formula that also stands at 2.269 (there μιν is Telemachus, here Penelope, who is the one addressed). φωνήσασ’ is the aorist participle of φωνέω ‘raise the voice’, and προσηύδα the imperfect of προσαυδάω ‘address’. ‘Winged words’ is translated the same every time.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ ἄγε δή μοι, μαῖα φίλη, νημερτὲς ἐνίσπες,
εἰ ἐτεὸν δὴ οἶκον ἱκάνεται, ὡς ἀγορεύεις,
ὅππως δὴ μνηστῆρσιν ἀναιδέσι χεῖρας ἐφῆκε
μοῦνος ἐών, οἱ δ’ αἰὲν ἀολλέες ἔνδον ἔμιμνον.
sentences.tr:
ei d’ age dē moi, maia philē, nēmertes enispes,
ei eteon dē oikon hikanetai, hōs agoreueis,
hoppōs dē mnēstērsin anaidesi cheiras ephēke
mounos eōn, hoi d’ aien aollees endon emimnon.
sentences.l:
“Come now, then, to me, dear nurse, unerringly tell,
if in truth he has come to his house, as you declare,
how upon the shameless suitors he laid hands,
alone being, while they ever in a crowd within stayed.”
sentences.i: “Come now, dear nurse, tell me unerringly: if he has truly come to his house, as you say, how he laid hands on the shameless suitors, alone as he was, while they stayed in the hall always together.”
sentences.n: εἰ δ’ ἄγε δή is 'come now'. ἐνίσπες is the aorist imperative of ἐνέπω 'tell'; νημερτές 'unerring' is used as an adverb and means that she wants what is true. What she is to tell is given in two indirect questions: 'if truly he has come' (εἰ ἐτεὸν δή, with εἰ meaning 'whether') and 'how' (ὅππως, an epic form of ὅπως). χεῖρας ἐφῆκε, 'let loose hands on', is the aorist of ἐφίημι and means 'attacked'. μοῦνος ἐών is 'being alone'. οἱ δ’ is a pronoun, 'they', and ἀολλέες is 'in a throng, together', and αἰέν (Ionic for ἀεί) is 'always'. ἀναιδέσι, 'shameless', is an epithet of the suitors. ἔμιμνον is the imperfect of μίμνω 'stay'.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε φίλη τροφὸς Εὐρύκλεια·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ aute proseeipe philē trophos Eurykleia·
sentences.l: Her then in turn addressed the dear nurse Eurycleia:
sentences.i: Then her dear nurse Eurycleia spoke to her in turn:
sentences.n: The same formula as line 25 (and 4.742); the English is the same.

sentences.t:
οὐκ ἴδον, οὐ πυθόμην, ἀλλὰ στόνον οἶον ἄκουσα
κτεινομένων·
sentences.tr:
ouk idon, ou pythomēn, alla stonon oion akousa
kteinomenōn·
sentences.l:
“I did not see, I did not learn, but a groan only I heard
of men being killed;
sentences.i: “I did not see it, and I did not learn of it; I only heard the groaning of men being killed;
sentences.n: ἴδον is the unaugmented aorist of ὁράω, 'saw' (Attic εἶδον), and πυθόμην the aorist of πυνθάνομαι 'learn, find out'. ἄκουσα is also unaugmented (Attic ἤκουσα). στόνον οἶον is 'a groan only'; οἶον is the accusative of οἶος 'alone'. στόνον is the object of ἄκουσα, and κτεινομένων, 'of those being killed', is a genitive participle that depends on it: 'the groan of men being killed'. The nurse says what she knows and what she does not.

sentences.t:
ἡμεῖς δὲ μυχῷ θαλάμων εὐπήκτων
ἥμεθ’ ἀτυζόμεναι, σανίδες δ’ ἔχον εὖ ἀραρυῖαι,
πρίν γ’ ὅτε δή με σὸς υἱὸς ἀπὸ μεγάροιο κάλεσσε
Τηλέμαχος·
sentences.tr:
hēmeis de mychōi thalamōn eupēktōn
hēmeth’ atyzomenai, sanides d’ echon eu araruiai,
prin g’ hote dē me sos huios apo megaroio kalesse
Tēlemachos·
sentences.l:
but we, in the recess of the well-built rooms,
sat terrified, and the boards held, well fitted,
until indeed me your son from the hall called,
Telemachus;
sentences.i: but we women sat terrified in the innermost part of the well-built rooms, and the well-fitted boards held, until your son called me out of the hall, Telemachus;
sentences.n: The sentence rests on ἥμεθ’, the imperfect of ἧμαι 'sit', elided; ἀτυζόμεναι is the feminine plural participle of ἀτύζομαι 'be stunned with fear', so 'we women'. μυχῷ is the dative of μυχός 'inner recess', and θαλάμων εὐπήκτων means 'well-built rooms' (εὐπηκτος, εὖ + πήγνυμι 'fix, fasten'). σανίδες are 'boards', probably the door-leaves, though the Greek does not say 'doors'; ἀραρυῖαι is a perfect participle of ἀραρίσκω 'fit together', agreeing with σανίδες. ἔχον, 'held', has no stated object. πρὶν γ’ ὅτε δή means 'until the time when'. σὸς υἱός is 'your son', and Τηλέμαχος stands last in apposition, delayed for effect. μεγάροιο is a genitive in -οιο. κάλεσσε is the aorist of καλέω, with doubled σ.

sentences.t: τὸν γάρ ῥα πατὴρ προέηκε καλέσσαι.
sentences.tr: ton gar rha patēr proeēke kalessai.
sentences.l: him, you see, his father had sent forth to call me.
sentences.i: for his father had sent him out to call me.
sentences.n: τόν is 'him', Telemachus. γάρ ῥα gives the reason: ῥα marks what follows naturally. προέηκε is the aorist of προΐημι 'send forth'; its object is Telemachus and its purpose is καλέσσαι, 'to call'. The same verb stands in line 51, with the nurse as the object.

sentences.t:
εὗρον ἔπειτ’ Ὀδυσῆα μετὰ κταμένοισι νέκυσσιν
ἑσταόθ’·
sentences.tr:
heuron epeit’ Odysēa meta ktamenoisi nekyssin
hestaoth’·
sentences.l:
I found then Odysseus among the slain corpses
standing;
sentences.i: I found Odysseus then, standing among the slain dead;
sentences.n: εὗρον is the unaugmented aorist of εὑρίσκω 'find'. κταμένοισι is the aorist middle participle of κτείνω, with passive sense 'slain'; both it and νέκυσσιν are datives (-οισι, -σσι). ἑσταόθ’ is the accusative of the perfect participle ἑσταώς, 'standing' (elided from ἑσταότα), agreeing with Ὀδυσῆα. It opens line 46, held back from Ὀδυσῆα in line 45, so that the figure stands out.

sentences.t:
οἱ δέ μιν ἀμφί, κραταίπεδον οὖδας ἔχοντες,
κείατ’ ἐπ’ ἀλλήλοισιν·
sentences.tr:
hoi de min amphi, krataipedon oudas echontes,
keiat’ ep’ allēloisin·
sentences.l:
and about him, the hard-floored ground holding,
lay on one another;
sentences.i: and around him, covering the hard floor, they lay heaped on one another;
sentences.n: οἱ δέ … ἔχοντες is 'and they, holding': the dead are the subject. μιν ἀμφί is ἀμφὶ μιν with the preposition after its noun. κραταίπεδον οὖδας is 'the hard-floored ground'; κραταίπεδος means 'with a strong floor', and οὖδας is the ground or floor. κείατ’ is κείατο, the epic imperfect 3 pl. of κεῖμαι 'lie' (Attic ἔκειντο), elided. ἀλλήλοισιν is the dative 'one another'.

sentences.t: ἰδοῦσά κε θυμὸν ἰάνθης.
sentences.tr: idousa ke thymon ianthēs.
sentences.l: Having seen, you would have been warmed in heart.
sentences.i: If you had seen them, your heart would have been warmed.
sentences.n: ἰδοῦσα is the aorist participle of ὁράω, 'having seen', and carries the condition. ἰάνθης is the aorist passive indicative, 2 sg., of ἰαίνω 'warm, cheer' (the accent marks the indicative, not a subjunctive); κε with the aorist indicative gives a past potential, 'you would have been'. θυμόν is an accusative of respect, 'in your heart'.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ οἱ μὲν δὴ πάντες ἐπ’ αὐλείῃσι θύρῃσιν
ἀθρόοι, αὐτὰρ ὁ δῶμα θεειοῦται περικαλλές,
πῦρ μέγα κηάμενος·
sentences.tr:
nyn d’ hoi men dē pantes ep’ auleiēisi thyrēisin
athrooi, autar ho dōma theeioutai perikalles,
pyr mega kēamenos·
sentences.i: But now they are all together at the courtyard doors, while he fumigates the very fair house with sulphur, having kindled a great fire;
sentences.n: Murray prints no line 49: the numbers pass from 48 to 50, and no word of the Greek is missing here. νῦν δέ sets the present against the scene just described. αὐλείῃσι θύρῃσιν is 'doors of the courtyard', with the dative in -ῃσι. ἀθρόοι is 'in a mass'. θεειοῦται is the present middle of θεειόω 'fumigate with sulphur' (θέειον), the cleaning of a place of death; the reader supplies 'with sulphur'. περικαλλές, 'very fair', is the stock epithet, translated the same each time, and the περι- is kept as 'very'. κηάμενος is the aorist middle participle of καίω 'burn', 'having lit'.

sentences.t: σὲ δέ με προέηκε καλέσσαι.
sentences.tr: se de me proeēke kalessai.
sentences.l: and you me he has sent forth to call.
sentences.i: and he has sent me out to call you.
sentences.n: σὲ δέ με sets the two persons side by side: 'you' is the object of the call and 'me' of the sending. The subject is ὁ, Odysseus, stated in line 50. προέηκε is the verb of line 44, now with the nurse as its object. The Greek is the same aorist in both lines, and the English verb is the same ('sent forth', 'sent … out'); only the time of speaking differs.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἕπευ, ὄφρα σφῶϊν ἐϋφροσύνης ἐπιβῆτον
ἀμφοτέρω φίλον ἦτορ, ἐπεὶ κακὰ πολλὰ πέποσθε.
sentences.tr:
all’ hepeu, ophra sphōïn eÿphrosynēs epibēton
amphoterō philon ētor, epei kaka polla peposthe.
sentences.l:
But follow, so that for you two of good cheer may take hold,
both, in the dear heart, since evils many you have suffered.
sentences.i: But follow me, so that both of you may come to good cheer in your dear hearts, since you have suffered many evils.
sentences.n: ἕπευ is the imperative middle of ἕπομαι 'follow' (Attic ἕπου). σφῶϊν and ἀμφοτέρω are dual forms: σφῶϊν is a dative-genitive ('for you two'), not a subject, and ἀμφοτέρω ('both') is the subject of ἐπιβῆτον, a dual aorist subjunctive of ἐπιβαίνω 'step upon' with the genitive ἐϋφροσύνης 'good cheer'; the grammar of the phrase is loose. φίλον ἦτορ is 'dear heart', in the singular for each of them. πέποσθε is the perfect of πάσχω with the epic 2 pl. ending (Attic πεπόνθατε).

sentences.t: νῦν δ’ ἤδη τόδε μακρὸν ἐέλδωρ ἐκτετέλεσται·
sentences.tr: nyn d’ ēdē tode makron eeldōr ektetelestai·
sentences.l: But now already this long wish has been fulfilled;
sentences.i: Now this long wish has already been fulfilled;
sentences.n: ἐέλδωρ is 'wish, longing'; it belongs to the family of ἔλδεαι in line 6, and the nurse takes up Penelope's own word. μακρόν is 'long': the wish has lasted a long time. ἐκτετέλεσται is the perfect passive of ἐκτελέω 'accomplish, fulfil'.

sentences.t:
ἦλθε μὲν αὐτὸς ζωὸς ἐφέστιος, εὗρε δὲ καὶ σὲ
καὶ παῖδ’ ἐν μεγάροισι·
sentences.tr:
ēlthe men autos zōos ephestios, heure de kai se
kai paid’ en megaroisi·
sentences.l:
He has come himself, alive, to his hearth, and found both you
and his son in the halls;
sentences.i: He has come himself, alive, to his hearth, and has found both you and his son in the halls;
sentences.n: ἐφέστιος is 'at, to the hearth' and so 'home'; the hearth is the heart of the house and the place of the household. ζωός is 'alive', in Ionic form. εὗρε is an aorist of εὑρίσκω. καὶ σὲ καὶ παῖδ’ is 'both you and the child'; παῖδ’ is elided παῖδα. ἐν μεγάροισι is the dative plural of μέγαρον, 'in the halls', with the plural used for one house.

sentences.t:
κακῶς δ’ οἵ πέρ μιν ἔρεζον
μνηστῆρες, τοὺς πάντας ἐτίσατο ᾧ ἐνὶ οἴκῳ.
sentences.tr:
kakōs d’ hoi per min erezon
mnēstēres, tous pantas etisato hōi eni oikōi.
sentences.l:
and badly those who treated him,
the suitors, all of those he punished in his own house.”
sentences.i: and the suitors who treated him ill, he has punished them all in his own house.”
sentences.n: κακῶς … ἔρεζον is 'treated him badly'; ἔρεζον is the imperfect of ῥέζω 'do', and the adverb with it makes 'treat'. οἵ πέρ μιν = 'those who … him', with the stress of περ. μνηστῆρες, the antecedent, follows the relative clause (a delayed noun), and τοὺς πάντας resumes it. ἐτίσατο is the aorist middle of τίνω, 'exacted payment from, punished'. ᾧ is the possessive ὅς, 'his own', and ἐνὶ is the Homeric form of ἐν; the phrase ᾧ ἐνὶ οἴκῳ is 'in his own house'.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε περίφρων Πηνελόπεια·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ aute proseeipe periphrōn Pēnelopeia·
sentences.l: Her then in turn addressed circumspect Penelope:
sentences.i: Then circumspect Penelope spoke to her in turn:
sentences.n: The same formula as line 10; the English is the same.

sentences.t: μαῖα φίλη, μή πω μέγ’ ἐπεύχεο καγχαλόωσα.
sentences.tr: maia philē, mē pō meg’ epeucheo kanchaloōsa.
sentences.l: “Dear nurse, do not yet loudly vaunt, exulting.
sentences.i: “Dear nurse, do not yet vaunt loudly, exulting.
sentences.n: μαῖα φίλη is the address of line 11, 'dear nurse'. ἐπεύχεο is the imperative of ἐπεύχομαι 'vaunt, boast aloud' (elsewhere the same verb is 'pray'), and μέγα is its adverb 'loudly'. καγχαλόωσα is the word of line 1: Penelope hands the nurse's own exultation back to her. μή πω means 'not yet'.

sentences.t:
οἶσθα γὰρ ὥς κ’ ἀσπαστὸς ἐνὶ μεγάροισι φανείη
πᾶσι, μάλιστα δ’ ἐμοί τε καὶ υἱέϊ, τὸν τεκόμεσθα·
sentences.tr:
oistha gar hōs k’ aspastos eni megaroisi phaneiē
pasi, malista d’ emoi te kai huieï, ton tekomestha·
sentences.l:
For you know how welcome in the halls he would appear
to all, and most of all to me and to the son whom we begot;
sentences.i: For you know how welcome he would be, appearing in the halls, to all, and most of all to me and to the son we begot;
sentences.n: οἶσθα is 'you know', the 2 sg. of οἶδα. The wording ὥς κ’ … φανείη is an indirect question with the optative, 'how he would appear'. ἀσπαστός is 'welcome'. υἱέϊ is a dative of υἱός. τεκόμεσθα is an aorist middle of τίκτω, 'we begot', without augment. The last words claim the son for both parents, in an unemphatic way.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἔσθ’ ὅδε μῦθος ἐτήτυμος, ὡς ἀγορεύεις,
ἀλλά τις ἀθανάτων κτεῖνε μνηστῆρας ἀγαυούς,
ὕβριν ἀγασσάμενος θυμαλγέα καὶ κακὰ ἔργα.
sentences.tr:
all’ ouk esth’ hode mythos etētymos, hōs agoreueis,
alla tis athanatōn kteine mnēstēras agauous,
hybrin agassamenos thymalgea kai kaka erga.
sentences.l:
but this tale is not true, as you declare,
but one of the immortals killed the noble suitors,
resenting their heart-grieving insolence and evil deeds.
sentences.i: But this tale is not true, as you say. One of the immortals killed the noble suitors, in indignation at their insolence, which grieved the heart, and at their evil deeds.
sentences.n: οὐκ ἔσθ’ is οὐκ ἔστι. ἐτήτυμος is 'true'; μῦθος is 'tale, story, report' here, not 'speech'. ἀγαυούς, 'noble', is the stock word of the suitors, translated every time. κτεῖνε is unaugmented (Attic ἔκτεινε). ἀγασσάμενος is the aorist participle of ἀγάομαι 'be indignant at', a word that elsewhere can mean 'admire'. ὕβριν is 'insolence', and θυμαλγέα 'heart-grieving' agrees with it. Penelope reasons that a god, not Odysseus, must have done it.

sentences.t:
οὔ τινα γὰρ τίεσκον ἐπιχθονίων ἀνθρώπων,
οὐ κακὸν οὐδὲ μὲν ἐσθλόν, ὅτις σφέας εἰσαφίκοιτο·
sentences.tr:
ou tina gar tieskon epichthoniōn anthrōpōn,
ou kakon oude men esthlon, hotis spheas eisaphikoito·
sentences.l:
for no one did they honour of men upon the earth,
neither bad nor yet good, whoever came to them;
sentences.i: for they honoured none of the men who live on the earth, neither bad nor good, whoever came to them;
sentences.n: τίεσκον is an iterative imperfect (-σκον) of τίω 'honour', 'they used to honour'. ἐπιχθονίων ἀνθρώπων, 'men upon the earth', is the fixed phrase for all mortals; it is translated every time. οὐ κακὸν οὐδὲ μὲν ἐσθλόν puts the two kinds of man in opposite columns. ὅτις σφέας εἰσαφίκοιτο is a general relative clause with the optative of εἰσαφικνέομαι 'come to'; σφέας is 'them'.

sentences.t: τῷ δι’ ἀτασθαλίας ἔπαθον κακόν·
sentences.tr: tōi di’ atasthalias epathon kakon·
sentences.l: therefore through wanton-follies they suffered evil;
sentences.i: so it was through wanton folly that they suffered evil;
sentences.n: τῷ is 'therefore' (the dative of the article as an adverb). δι’ ἀτασθαλίας is διά with the accusative plural, 'on account of wanton follies' (the form could also be a genitive singular, 'through wanton folly'; the sense is the same), the same word as in 1.7, with the same English. ἔπαθον is the aorist of πάσχω 'suffer'. The ending · ends the thought; the next unit begins with αὐτάρ.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ὀδυσσεὺς
ὤλεσε τηλοῦ νόστον Ἀχαιΐδος, ὤλετο δ’ αὐτός.
sentences.tr:
autar Odysseus
ōlese tēlou noston Achaiïdos, ōleto d’ autos.
sentences.l:
but Odysseus
lost, far from the Achaean land, his homecoming, and perished himself.”
sentences.i: but Odysseus lost his homecoming far from the land of the Achaeans, and perished himself.”
sentences.n: αὐτάρ is 'but'. ὤλεσε is the aorist active of ὄλλυμι 'destroy, lose', and ὤλετο its aorist middle, 'perished'; the same verb is used twice, with two meanings, and the echo is the point. τηλοῦ takes the genitive Ἀχαιΐδος, 'far from the Achaean land' (Ἀχαιΐς is the land of the Achaeans, that is Greece). νόστον is 'homecoming'. αὐτός is 'himself'.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα φίλη τροφὸς Εὐρύκλεια·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ ēmeibet’ epeita philē trophos Eurykleia·
sentences.l: Her then answered the dear nurse Eurycleia:
sentences.i: Then her dear nurse Eurycleia answered her:
sentences.n: τὴν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα is the standing formula for an answer, 'her then answered'. ἠμείβετο is the imperfect middle of ἀμείβομαι 'reply'. The reply-verbs are not the same: 'in turn' belongs to αὖτε, which is not used here. The nurse is called by her fixed name φίλη τροφός, 'dear nurse'.

sentences.t:
τέκνον ἐμόν, ποῖόν σε ἔπος φύγεν ἕρκος ὀδόντων,
ἣ πόσιν ἔνδον ἐόντα παρ’ ἐσχάρῃ οὔ ποτ’ ἔφησθα
οἴκαδ’ ἐλεύσεσθαι·
sentences.tr:
teknon emon, poion se epos phygen herkos odontōn,
hē posin endon eonta par’ escharēi ou pot’ ephēstha
oikad’ eleusesthai·
sentences.i: “My child, what a word is this that has got past the fence of your teeth, you who said that your husband, though he is in the house by the hearth, would never come home;
sentences.n: The first words repeat 1.64, which ends there with a full stop. ἕρκος ὀδόντων, 'the fence of your teeth', is the image of speech as a thing that should be held in by the teeth, and it is kept every time. ποῖον is 'of what sort', in an exclamation. φύγεν is the unaugmented aorist of φεύγω, with σε as its object. ἣ … ἔφησθα takes up σε: 'you who said'. ἔφησθα is the 2 sg. of φημί, in an old form. The participle ἐόντα has concessive force in the English, 'though he is'. After a verb of saying the negative οὔ ποτε goes with the infinitive in meaning: 'said he would never come'. παρ’ ἐσχάρῃ, 'by the hearth', is a dative, and οἴκαδε means 'homewards'.

sentences.t: θυμὸς δέ τοι αἰὲν ἄπιστος.
sentences.tr: thymos de toi aien apistos.
sentences.l: but your heart is ever unbelieving.
sentences.i: Your heart has always been unbelieving.
sentences.n: θυμός is the heart or spirit as the seat of feeling. τοι is the dative of σύ, 'your'. αἰέν is the Ionic form of ἀεί, 'always'. ἄπιστος is 'not trusting, unbelieving'; it has the same root as πίστις 'trust', and it describes Penelope's character. The nurse is blunt.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε τοι καὶ σῆμα ἀριφραδὲς ἄλλο τι εἴπω,
οὐλήν, τήν ποτέ μιν σῦς ἤλασε λευκῷ ὀδόντι.
sentences.tr:
all’ age toi kai sēma ariphrades allo ti eipō,
oulēn, tēn pote min sys ēlase leukōi odonti.
sentences.l:
But come, to you also a sign, very plain, another, let me tell,
the scar, which once him a boar struck with a white tooth.
sentences.i: But come, let me tell you another sign as well, a very plain one: the scar, which a boar had once struck him with its white tusk.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε is 'but come', and εἴπω is the aorist subjunctive, 1 sg., a hortatory 'let me tell'. σῆμα is a sign, a token; ἀριφραδές 'very plain' has the intensive ἀρι- and the root of φράζω 'point out'. The second line repeats 19.393; οὐλήν is 'scar', the stock word. ἤλασε is the aorist of ἐλαύνω 'drive, strike'. λευκῷ ὀδόντι, 'with a white tooth', is a boar's tusk.

sentences.t:
τὴν ἀπονίζουσα φρασάμην, ἔθελον δὲ σοὶ αὐτῇ
εἰπέμεν·
sentences.tr:
tēn aponizousa phrasamēn, ethelon de soi autēi
eipemen·
sentences.l:
This, while washing, I noticed, and I wished to you yourself
to tell;
sentences.i: I noticed it while I was washing him, and I wanted to tell you yourself;
sentences.n: τήν is the article as a pronoun, 'it', the scar. ἀπονίζουσα is a participle of ἀπονίζω 'wash off', and the object, 'him', is left to be understood: the scene is the washing of his feet. φρασάμην is the aorist middle of φράζω, 'I noticed, I took note of'. ἔθελον is 'I wished', and εἰπέμεν is the aorist infinitive (Attic εἰπεῖν) with the epic ending -μεν. σοὶ αὐτῇ is 'to you yourself'.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά με κεῖνος ἑλὼν ἐπὶ μάστακα χερσὶν
οὐκ ἔα εἰπέμεναι πολυϊδρείῃσι νόοιο.
sentences.tr:
alla me keinos helōn epi mastaka chersin
ouk ea eipemenai polyïdreiēisi nooio.
sentences.l:
but me that man, taking hold on my jaws with his hands,
did not allow to tell, by the great knowing of his mind.
sentences.i: But that man put his hands to my mouth and would not let me tell you, because of the cunning of his mind.
sentences.n: κεῖνος is ἐκεῖνος, 'that man'. ἑλών is the aorist participle of αἱρέω 'seize'. μάστακα is 'mouth, jaws', that is, the part one chews with; the nurse is saying that he stopped her mouth. ἔα is the epic imperfect of ἐάω 'allow' (Attic εἴα), and εἰπέμεναι is the infinitive with the ending -μεναι. πολυϊδρείῃσι is the plural dative of πολυϊδρείη, 'much knowledge, cunning', with νόοιο, a genitive in -οιο, 'of his mind'. The dative says why: from the cunning of his mind.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἕπευ·
sentences.tr: all’ hepeu·
sentences.l: But follow;
sentences.i: But follow me;
sentences.n: ἕπευ is the same imperative as in line 52. After the aside, she repeats the invitation.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼν ἐμέθεν περιδώσομαι αὐτῆς,
αἴ κέν σ’ ἐξαπάφω, κτεῖναί μ’ οἰκτίστῳ ὀλέθρῳ.
sentences.tr:
autar egōn emethen peridōsomai autēs,
ai ken s’ exapaphō, kteinai m’ oiktistōi olethrōi.
sentences.l:
and I will stake my own self on it,
if I deceive you, to kill me by a most pitiable death.”
sentences.i: And I will stake my very self on it: if I deceive you, kill me by the most pitiable death.”
sentences.n: αὐτάρ is 'but, and'. περιδώσομαι is the future middle of περιδίδωμι (περιδίδομαι) 'stake, wager', and ἐμέθεν αὐτῆς is 'my very self' (ἐμέθεν is the genitive of ἐγώ, αὐτῆς 'itself'). αἴ κέν is 'if'. ἐξαπάφω is the aorist subjunctive of ἐξαπαφίσκω 'deceive'. The infinitive κτεῖναι stands for an imperative, 'kill', a use of the infinitive that Homer allows. οἰκτίστῳ ὀλέθρῳ is 'by a most pitiable death'; οἰκτίστῳ is the superlative of οἰκτρός, which is kept as 'most pitiable' every time.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα περίφρων Πηνελόπεια·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ ēmeibet’ epeita periphrōn Pēnelopeia·
sentences.l: Her then answered circumspect Penelope:
sentences.i: Then circumspect Penelope answered her:
sentences.n: The reply-formula, with ἠμείβετο 'answered', now said of Penelope. The line repeats the first line of the unit at 4.808, and the English follows that line. Circumspect is her stock epithet and is translated every time.

sentences.t:
μαῖα φίλη, χαλεπόν σε θεῶν αἰειγενετάων
δήνεα εἴρυσθαι, μάλα περ πολύϊδριν ἐοῦσαν.
sentences.tr:
maia philē, chalepon se theōn aieigenetaōn
dēnea eirysthai, mala per polyïdrin eousan.
sentences.l:
“Dear nurse, hard it is for you, of the gods who are forever-born,
the counsels to ward off, very much-knowing though you are.
sentences.i: “Dear nurse, it is hard for you to ward off the counsels of the everlasting gods, very knowing though you are.
sentences.n: χαλεπόν is 'hard' with an unstated ἐστί, and σε is the accusative subject of the infinitive: 'for you to …'. θεῶν αἰειγενετάων is 'of the gods who are born for ever', that is everlasting; this is a different word from the formula θεοὶ αἰὲν ἐόντες. δήνεα is a poetic word for 'counsels, designs'. εἴρυσθαι is an infinitive of ἐρύομαι, which means 'protect, ward off'. The sense of the whole phrase is not sure: the likeliest reading is that even a very shrewd person cannot keep out the gods' plans. πολύϊδριν ἐοῦσαν 'being very knowing' is the participle ἐοῦσαν, Ionic for οὖσαν, with πολύϊδρις, 'knowing much', the same root as πολυϊδρείῃσι in line 77.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἔμπης ἴομεν μετὰ παῖδ’ ἐμόν, ὄφρα ἴδωμαι
ἄνδρας μνηστῆρας τεθνηότας, ἠδ’ ὃς ἔπεφνεν.
sentences.tr:
all’ empēs iomen meta paid’ emon, ophra idōmai
andras mnēstēras tethnēotas, ēd’ hos epephnen.
sentences.l:
But all the same let us go to my son, so that I may see
the men, the suitors, dead, and him who slew them.”
sentences.i: But all the same, let us go to my son, so that I may see the suitors lying dead, and the one who killed them.”
sentences.n: ἔμπης is 'nevertheless'. ἴομεν is the subjunctive of εἶμι 'go', 'let us go'. ὄφρα ἴδωμαι is 'so that I may see'. ἄνδρας μνηστῆρας is 'the men, the suitors', in apposition; the dead are called 'suitors' with no epithet here. τεθνηότας is the perfect participle of θνῄσκω, 'dead'. ἠδ’ ὅς ἔπεφνεν is 'and the one who killed', the killer left unnamed. ἔπεφνεν is the reduplicated aorist of φένω 'slay'.

sentences.t: ὣς φαμένη κατέβαιν’ ὑπερώϊα·
sentences.tr: hōs phamenē katebain’ hyperōïa·
sentences.l: So saying, she went down from the upper rooms;
sentences.i: So saying, she came down from the upper rooms;
sentences.n: ὣς φαμένη is 'so saying' (φαμένη is the participle middle of φημί). κατέβαιν’ is the imperfect κατέβαινε, elided, 'was going down'. ὑπερώϊα is the same 'upper rooms' as ὑπερῷ’ in line 1, here with the accusative of place alone: she goes down out of them. The nurse climbed up in line 1, laughing; the mistress comes down in doubt.

sentences.t:
πολλὰ δέ οἱ κῆρ
ὥρμαιν’, ἢ ἀπάνευθε φίλον πόσιν ἐξερεείνοι,
ἦ παρστᾶσα κύσειε κάρη καὶ χεῖρε λαβοῦσα.
sentences.tr:
polla de hoi kēr
hōrmain’, ē apaneuthe philon posin exereeinoi,
ē parstasa kyseie karē kai cheire labousa.
sentences.l:
and much her heart
was debating, whether apart she should question her dear husband,
or standing by should kiss his head and hands, taking them.
sentences.i: and her heart debated much whether to keep apart and question her dear husband, or to go up to him and kiss his head and take his hands.
sentences.n: πολλά is an adverb, 'much'. οἱ is the dative of the person, 'her'. κῆρ is 'heart' as the seat of feeling. ὥρμαινε is the imperfect of ὁρμαίνω 'turn over in the mind, debate'. ἢ … ἦ are 'whether … or' (ἦ is ἤ), each with the optative of indirect deliberation: ἐξερεείνοι, 'she should question', and κύσειε, 'she should kiss' (aorist of κυνέω). ἀπάνευθε is 'at a distance'. φίλον πόσιν is 'dear husband'. παρστᾶσα is the aorist participle of παρίστημι, 'standing beside', and χεῖρε is a dual, 'the two hands'.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ ἐπεὶ εἰσῆλθεν καὶ ὑπέρβη λάϊνον οὐδόν,
ἕζετ’ ἔπειτ’ Ὀδυσῆος ἐναντίη, ἐν πυρὸς αὐγῇ,
τοίχου τοῦ ἑτέρου·
sentences.tr:
hē d’ epei eisēlthen kai hyperbē laïnon oudon,
hezet’ epeit’ Odysēos enantiē, en pyros augēi,
toichou tou heterou·
sentences.i: And when she had come in and stepped over the stone threshold, she sat down opposite Odysseus, in the light of the fire, by the other wall;
sentences.n: εἰσῆλθεν is an aorist of εἰσέρχομαι 'go in'. ὑπέρβη is the unaugmented aorist of ὑπερβαίνω 'step over'. λάϊνον is 'of stone' (from λᾶας), and οὐδός is the 'threshold'. ἕζετο is 'sat down'. ἐναντίη is the feminine of ἐναντίος 'opposite', agreeing with the subject and taking the genitive Ὀδυσῆος; Ὀδυσῆος is the Ionic genitive. ἐν πυρὸς αὐγῇ is 'in the gleam of the fire'. τοίχου τοῦ ἑτέρου is 'by the other wall' with a genitive of the place where.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ ἄρα πρὸς κίονα μακρὴν
ἧστο κάτω ὁρόων, ποτιδέγμενος εἴ τί μιν εἴποι
ἰφθίμη παράκοιτις, ἐπεὶ ἴδεν ὀφθαλμοῖσιν.
sentences.tr:
ho d’ ara pros kiona makrēn
hēsto katō horoōn, potidegmenos ei ti min eipoi
iphthimē parakoitis, epei iden ophthalmoisin.
sentences.l:
and he by a tall pillar
was sitting, looking down, waiting whether anything to him
she would say, his mighty consort, when she saw him with her eyes.
sentences.i: while he sat by a tall pillar, looking down, waiting to see whether his mighty wife would say anything to him, once she had seen him with her eyes.
sentences.n: ὁ δ’ ἄρα is 'and he'. κίονα μακρήν is 'tall pillar', with πρός and the accusative. ἧστο is the imperfect of ἧμαι 'sit'. ὁρόων is the uncontracted ὁρῶν, and κάτω ὁρόων is 'looking down'. ποτιδέγμενος is the middle participle of ποτιδέχομαι (= προσδέχομαι), 'waiting for'. εἴ τί μιν εἴποι is an indirect question with the optative of εἶπον: 'whether she would say anything to him'. ἰφθίμη, 'mighty', is a stock epithet for a woman and is translated every time, though it sits oddly here; παράκοιτις is 'consort', kept as 'wife' in the free English. ἴδεν is unaugmented (Attic εἶδεν), and ὀφθαλμοῖσιν is a dative plural.

sentences.t: ἡ δ’ ἄνεω δὴν ἧστο, τάφος δέ οἱ ἦτορ ἵκανεν·
sentences.tr: hē d’ aneō dēn hēsto, taphos de hoi ētor hikanen·
sentences.l: And she a long while sat silent, and amazement her heart reached;
sentences.i: She sat a long while without a word, and amazement reached her heart;
sentences.n: ἡ δ’ is 'and she', Penelope. ἄνεω is 'speechless, silent'. δήν is 'a long time'. ἧστο is the same 'sat' as in the line before. τάφος is 'amazement, stupor', a different word from τάφος 'grave'. οἱ is the dative, 'her'. ἦτορ is the 'heart' as a seat of feeling. ἵκανεν is the imperfect of ἱκάνω 'reach, come to'. The silence continues for the rest of the part.

sentences.t:
ὄψει δ’ ἄλλοτε μέν μιν ἐνωπαδίως ἐσίδεσκεν,
ἄλλοτε δ’ ἀγνώσασκε κακὰ χροῒ εἵματ’ ἔχοντα.
sentences.tr:
opsei d’ allote men min enōpadiōs esidesken,
allote d’ agnōsaske kaka chroï heimat’ echonta.
sentences.l:
and at one time with her eyes face to face she would look at him,
at another time she would fail to know him, bad clothes upon his skin wearing.
sentences.i: At one moment she would look straight at him, at another she would fail to know him, wearing, as he did, shabby clothes on his body.
sentences.n: ὄψει δ’ ἄλλοτε μέν … ἄλλοτε δ’ is 'at one time … at another time'; ὄψει is a dative, 'by sight, with her eyes'. ἐνωπαδίως is 'face to face, straight on'. ἐσίδεσκεν and ἀγνώσασκε have the iterative suffix -σκε(ν), 'she would look', 'she would fail to know' (from εἰσοράω and ἀγνοέω). μιν is 'him'. κακὰ χροῒ εἵματ’ ἔχοντα is 'having bad clothes on his skin'. χροῒ is a dative of χρώς 'skin, body', and ἔχοντα agrees with μιν.

sentences.t: Τηλέμαχος δ’ ἐνένιπεν ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζε·
sentences.tr: Tēlemachos d’ enenipen epos t’ ephat’ ek t’ onomaze·
sentences.l: and Telemachus rebuked her and spoke a word and called her by name:
sentences.i: Telemachus rebuked her, and spoke, calling her by name:
sentences.n: This line introduces a speech that begins in the next part, so no quotation mark stands here. ἐνένιπεν is the aorist of ἐνίπτω 'rebuke'; its object, Penelope, is not stated. The formula ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζε is 'and spoke a word, and called by name', and the free English drops 'a word' for fluency. What he says comes in the next part.
